doc.title: Houston Person Part 1 interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Influences: R&B, gospel and the church
title: Significant tone, authority and blues emotion
summary: Woods tells of a deacon urging a singer to do something with the melody; they discuss authority, inflection, the blues, and combining emotion with musicianship.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: You know you mentioned changing inflection, and there’s a concept that I teach in my classes called significant tone. In other words, from African American community, like if you went to a black Baptist or black Pentecostal church, and you got up to sing “Amazing Grace,” and you sing it straight, and I heard this happen in a church one time, a girl got up and sang it straight cause she was worried about, oh, what will people think. And one of the deacons touched her on the arm and said, “look baby, we already know the melody.”
“Now convince me that you know what grace is, come on, do something with that melody.”

Yeah, it’s a certain authority that you have to have. You can hear that most of that, well I guess you call, well in the English language I guess there’s words for all these things, indigenous cultures I guess, like country & western music. The lyrics to their songs are so basic and down to earth, you can’t miss the message. Then you’ve got to do something with it. And then when they add the inflections and the tones that they use, you know, you know what they mean, it’s just real. And I guess it’s almost sometimes like the blues really, cause they use the same words. Like you said “y’all” and certain words that let you know that we are from the same place.
Uh huh. A sense of community.
You know I was thinking of the blues for a tremendous emotional vehicle where the subjective qualities have to be exalted over the object of desire, cause it ain’t but twelve bars.

That’s right, and as you said before, the emotion is first. And with jazz, in a lot of instances, the musicianship comes first. Now where my thing is, where I try to bring emotion and musicianship together, that’s about where I am.
